opus-5.5.text:
Cambridge appealed to me for a few reasons, and honestly some of them only became clear after I visited.

The first is the density of people. Within a short walk or bike ride you have researchers working on almost everything: mathematics, computer science, physics, biology, philosophy. You go to a seminar, or just sit down at lunch in college, and you end up talking to someone whose work is completely different from yours but somehow connects. That kind of accidental collision is hard to engineer anywhere else, and I've found it shapes how I think about problems.

The second is the tradition, though not in a museum sense. When you walk past the buildings where certain ideas were first worked out, it reminds you that research is a long conversation across generations. You feel you're contributing a small piece to something much bigger, and that's quite motivating.

Third, the pace. Compared with some places I've been, Cambridge leaves room to think. There's pressure, of course, but there's also a culture that respects slow, deep work: spending a long time on a hard question rather than chasing whatever is fashionable this quarter. As a young faculty member, that freedom matters a lot to me.

And finally the students. Teaching through the supervision system, sitting with two or three undergraduates and working through problems together, keeps me honest. They ask questions I thought I understood, and often I realize I didn't. That's been one of the most rewarding parts of the job.

So it was a mix of the intellectual environment, the freedom to pursue long-term questions, and the people. It felt like a place where I could grow, not just a place to do my job.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the first thing was the people. When I visited, I spent a day just walking between offices and labs, and every conversation drifted somewhere I didn't expect. Someone working on protein folding would end up talking about information theory, and then a historian of science would wander in and complicate both of us. That kind of casual cross-pollination is rare, and at Cambridge it felt like the default rather than something you had to engineer.

The second thing was the time horizon. A lot of places, implicitly or explicitly, want you to show results in two or three years. Cambridge still has this culture where it's acceptable to say, "I'm chasing something that might take a decade, and I'm not sure it will work." The college system contributes to that. You have dinner with people who've been thinking about one problem for thirty years, and it recalibrates your sense of what a career can look like.

And then, I'll admit, there's the romance of it. You bike past buildings where Newton and Turing worked. That sounds like a cliché, but it does something to you. It makes you a little more ambitious and a little more humble at the same time, which I think is the right mixture for doing research.

I was also drawn to the fact that it's not London. It's small enough that you run into collaborators at the market, but close enough to London that the wider world is an hour away. For me, that balance between quiet and connection was exactly what I wanted at this stage.

astra-6.text: What appealed to me was the intellectual environment—the chance to be around people asking interesting questions, including people outside my own field. When you’re choosing a faculty position, you’re also choosing a community: the colleagues you’ll learn from and the students you’ll work with. Cambridge felt like a place where I could keep growing intellectually while building something of my own.

sol-6.1.text: What appealed to me was the intellectual environment—the chance to be surrounded by people asking interesting questions and approaching them from different perspectives. I also liked the idea of being somewhere with such a strong connection between teaching and research. Having talented students and colleagues who challenge your thinking seemed like a very good reason to come.
